newsitem.title: USA: U.S.,Turkey to discuss economic problems over Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S.,Turkey to discuss economic problems over Iraq.

text.p: The United States will hold talks with Turkey early next week on Turkish economic losses resulting from U.S. action against Iraq and related issues, the State Department said on Friday.

Spokesman Glyn Davies said U.S. Ambassador to Ankara Marc Grossman would discuss the issues with the Turkish government. Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said earlier that she wanted compensation from the United States for losses incurred by her country's backing for the Western effort against Iraq.

"It's about time the United States proved they also stand by Turkey -- these losses have to be compensated," Ciller told BBC World television. "We only want a certain portion of our losses to be compensated economically."

A plan for Iraq to export oil through a Turkish pipeline, bringing Turkey much-needed revenues, has been put on hold after Iraq's military move into Western-protected Kurdistan last week and retaliatory U.S. missile strikes.
Davies told a news briefing Ciller had raised Turkey's economic problems in letters on Sept. 1 to U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and on Sept. 4 to President Bill Clinton.

"She did flag Turkish concern over the impact of the cancellation temporarily of (U.N. Security Council Resolution) 986 and other economic hardships and she indicated a desire to have consultations, which we will have with the Turkish government," he said.

Davies could not confirm that Ciller had asked specifically for compensation. But he said the United States "is well aware of Turkish concerns, given the hardships that Turkey has suffered as a result of the loss of trade with Iraq. We're very mindful of that."
Iraq has been under United Nations economic sanctions since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Davies said Grossman's talks were expected also to cover Operation Provide Comfort, under which Western warplanes enforce a no-fly-zone over northern Iraq to protect Kurds there against Baghdad, and Turkey's plan to create a buffer zone in northern Iraq.

Davies admitted that the past week's events had changed the situation in northern Iraq, forcing the withdrawal of ground-based personnel involved in Provide Comfort, which operates out of Incirlik airbase in southeastern Turkey.
But, he said: "We want very much for Provide Comfort to go forward and expect it will."

The United States said on Thursday it did not object to a Turkish plan to establish a three-to-six mile (5-10 km) wide security zone in northern Iraq after Ankara said it would be short-lived and not involve the stationing of Turkish troops.
Ankara says it wants the zone to protect itself against infiltration by separatist Kurdish guerrillas based in northern Iraq.
